summary: Proposes two changes to the IMP-to-Host protocol to improve communication between users and the network: expanding the Host-Going-Down message and adding a Dead-Host-Status message.

plainLanguage.summary: The network box can tell a computer when others are going down. These two changes make that news clearer and more useful.

questions: why did arpanet hosts need status codes
subtitle: Enhanced IMP-to-Host messages for better host status communication

tldr.problem: When ARPANET hosts needed to shut down, they could send a message to their IMP saying they were going down, but they had no way to say when they would be back or why they were shutting down. Similarly, IMPs could tell hosts that a remote host was down, but could not explain why.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes expanding the Host-Going-Down message to include the time of day and day of week when the host will come back up, plus a reason code (scheduled maintenance, emergency restart, hardware failure, power outage, etc.). It also adds a new Dead Host Status message that allows IMPs to send the same status information to source hosts when a destination host is unreachable.
tldr.outcome: Network operators and users gained better visibility into host availability, allowing more intelligent routing decisions and giving users better information about when services would return.

facts.label: Message type for Dead Host Status

today: RFC 611 documents an incremental improvement to the ARPANET's IMP/Host protocol. While the ARPANET itself is now historical, the concepts it established—communicating host status, providing reason codes, and handling status mismatches—remain relevant to modern network protocols and server health monitoring systems.

sections.title: The Problem: Silent Shutdowns
sections.content:
The original IMP/Host protocol allowed a host to send a Host-Going-Down message to its IMP to announce that it was shutting down, but the message had no fields for additional information. Network operators and users would see a host disappear, with no explanation of whether it was intentional maintenance, a crash, a power failure, or something else. They had no way to know when the host would return.

For remote users trying to access that host, or for system administrators managing network traffic, this lack of information was frustrating and inefficient. Operators at the Network Control Center (NCC) might spend time trying to diagnose problems that were actually just scheduled maintenance.
sections.plainLanguage: When a computer shut down, it would say so, but it couldn't say why or when it would come back. That was confusing for everyone waiting for it to come back.

sections.title: Two Protocol Enhancements
sections.content:
The RFC proposes two complementary changes to the IMP/Host protocol.

First, expand the Host-Going-Down message (type 2) to include two new pieces of information. Bits 17-28 encode the time when the host will come back up (the day of the week, the hour of the day, and the 5-minute interval within that hour, all in Universal Time/GMT). Bits 29-32 provide a reason code: values 0-4 are reserved for IMP use, but hosts can specify scheduled PM maintenance, scheduled hardware work, scheduled software work, emergency restart, power outage, software breakpoint, or hardware failure. If a host doesn't know when it will come back, it can set bits 17-27 all to ones and bit 28 to zero.

Second, add a new Dead Host Status message (type 6) that the IMP can send to a source host to explain why a destination host is unreachable. This message carries the same timing and reason code information, allowing the source host to inform its users of what happened to the destination host. The RFC specifies different reason codes for Dead Host Status, ranging from "IMP has no information" to specific causes like hardware failure, power outage, or scheduled maintenance.
sections.plainLanguage: Now a shutting-down computer can say when it will be back and why (like "we are fixing the hardware" or "power went out"). Also, when one computer asks another and finds it is down, the network can explain why it is down.

sections.title: Deployment and Compatibility
sections.content:
The RFC notes that these modifications were to be deployed "very soon" and urges hosts to implement the new message types as quickly as possible. The changes are mostly backward compatible, with one exception: older hosts that had not been updated would receive type 6 (Dead Host Status) messages they did not know how to handle, and would likely log these as errors.

The RFC recommends that the NCC retain the Host-Going-Down message even after a host has shut down, so it can tell local users who try to access the down host why it is unavailable and when it will return. The NCC could even update the message by phone if a host took longer to restart than originally expected.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone was supposed to start using these new messages soon. Some old computers might be confused by the new message types at first, but that was okay. The network staff could also change a shutdown message if the computer ended up taking longer to come back than it said.
